lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you learned latitude and longitude. What is the latitude of the equator? (0°.) Today: why every flat map stretches the globe, and how to choose the right map for a job.

The Earth is a ball, so only a globe shows every size, shape and distance truly. Try to flatten an orange peel: it tears or stretches. A map projection is a way of flattening the globe; each keeps some things true and stretches others.

Gerardus Mercator's map of 1569 keeps directions true: a straight line is a steady compass course, perfect for sailors. But it stretches sizes towards the poles: lengths 2 times at 60°, so areas there look 4 times too big.

On a Mercator map Greenland looks about as big as Africa. In fact Africa is about 14 times bigger: about 30 million km² against about 2.2 million. Web maps on phones use a kind of Mercator too, because it keeps shapes right as you zoom.

Equal-area maps, such as the Gall-Peters, show every country's true size, so Africa looks as big as it really is. But shapes near the equator look tall and stretched, and near the poles squashed flat.

Compromise maps, such as the Robinson projection (1963), bend the edges so nothing is very wrong: good for wall maps. Azimuthal maps centre on one point and keep true distances from it; the United Nations' emblem uses one centred on the North Pole.

Choose a map for its job. Mercator is for steering by compass, equal-area for comparing sizes, and compromise for a wall map. Azimuthal is for distances from one place. Ask what a map keeps true, and what it stretches.

Try it in the world: make a map of your village that keeps distances true: pace out each path and draw it to scale. Then try to wrap a flat square around a round hill: where does it crumple? Next: a GIS investigation.

exercises.prompt: Only a globe shows every size and shape truly.
exercises.hint: Think what happens when you flatten an orange peel.
exercises.explain: True: every flat map stretches the globe somewhere.

exercises.prompt: What does a Mercator map keep true?
exercises.hint: It was made for sailors in 1569.
exercises.explain: Directions: a straight line on it is a steady compass course.

exercises.prompt: Africa is about 30.4 million km² and Greenland about 2.2 million km². About how many times bigger is Africa? Round to a whole number.
exercises.hint: Divide Africa's area by Greenland's, then round.

exercises.prompt: Which map shows every country's true size?
choices: a street map of one town
exercises.hint: Its name tells you what it keeps equal.
exercises.explain: An equal-area map, such as the Gall-Peters.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of map to what it keeps true.
exercises.hint: Directions, sizes, distances, and a balance.
exercises.explain: Mercator: directions. Equal-area: sizes. Azimuthal: distances from its centre. Compromise: a balance.

exercises.prompt: At 60° Mercator stretches lengths 2 times, both east-west and north-south. How many times too big do areas there look?
exercises.hint: An area stretches both ways: multiply.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: what does a Mercator map do well, and what does it get wrong?
exercises.hint: It keeps directions and small shapes; it stretches sizes near the poles.
exercises.explain: Well: compass courses, small shapes, zooming. Wrong: Greenland's and Antarctica's sizes, and the poles.

exercises.prompt: Why do web maps on phones use a kind of Mercator?
choices: it keeps shapes right when you zoom
exercises.hint: Think of zooming into a street corner.
exercises.explain: It keeps shapes and angles right close up, so streets look right as you zoom.

exercises.prompt: Put these places in order of how much Mercator stretches them, least first.
exercises.hint: The nearer the pole, the bigger the stretch.

exercises.prompt: On a Mercator map, Greenland looks far smaller than it really is.
exercises.hint: Remember what Mercator does near the poles.
exercises.explain: False: it looks far bigger than it really is.

exercises.prompt: Which map would you choose to compare the sizes of African and European countries?
choices: an azimuthal map of the North Pole
exercises.hint: The job is comparing sizes fairly.
exercises.explain: An equal-area map: every country at its true size, so the comparison is fair.

exercises.prompt: A country at 60° N looks 8 million km² on a Mercator map, where areas look 4 times too big. What is its true area, in million km²?
exercises.hint: Divide how big it looks by the stretch of areas.

exercises.prompt: Why can no flat map be perfect?
choices: a ball cannot be flattened without stretching
exercises.explain: A sphere's surface cannot lie flat without stretching or tearing, so every map distorts something.

exercises.prompt: Sort these jobs: which kind of map is best?
exercises.hint: Directions, fair sizes, or distances from one point?
exercises.explain: Mercator: sailing, sea voyages. Equal-area: farmland, population. Azimuthal: flights from the Pole, radio distances.

exercises.prompt: The United Nations' emblem shows an azimuthal map centred on the North Pole.
exercises.hint: Look back at the card about compromise and azimuthal maps.
exercises.explain: True: its map is centred on the North Pole, with olive branches round it.
